paper_title: E-Commerce Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Business Operation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon agentic tasks go beyond chaining short tasks over more interaction turns. Their evolving dynamic environments and long-range dependencies require Large Language Models (LLMs) to continually explore, learn from experience, and adapt their policies over thousands of steps. We introduce E-Commerce Bench, the first open-source benchmark that integrates multi-round counterpart negotiation and dynamic events into a year-long business operation. Over a 365-day year, an LLM agent concurrently runs multiple online stores, researching the market, negotiating with suppliers to source inventory, optimizing sales strategies, fulfilling orders, handling returns, and managing cash flow to maximize its end-of-year total assets. To construct a realistic merchant-side operating environment, the product and supplier data are derived from a real e-commerce platform, while a year-long calendar of promotions, natural disasters, and supply-chain shocks continually reshapes demand. For reproducibility, both sides of the market are deterministic: customer purchases and returns follow a fixed demand model, while a negotiation kernel determines supplier pricing, concessions, and decisions, with an LLM used only to verbalize them. We evaluate 18 frontier models across seven dimensions, including year-end assets, and find that no single model dominates. GPT-5.6 Sol earns the most, growing the 100,000 opening stake into 1,431,425, yet it ranks 16th of 18 on fraud avoidance and trails Fable5 in operational efficiency. Among open-weight models, Qwen3.8-Max-Preview leads with 416,252, 38% above GLM 5.2 (high), and achieves the strongest learning over the horizon, progressively bargaining down prices across repeated orders. Our code is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/E-CommerceBench.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to handle tasks that span thousands of steps, planning and acting over long trajectories with external tools (Yao et al., 2023). Such tasks require an agent to make sequential decisions, adapt to past experiences, and remain coherent long after the initial instruction. Sustained competence of this kind marks frontier for current models and eludes most agentic benchmarks. In reinforcement learning, tasks are divided into episodic and continuing ones (Sutton & Barto, 2018), and this distinction also organizes the long-horizon agentic tasks. Episodic benchmarks set goal and score its completion, whether resolving GitHub issue (Jimenez et al., 2024), operating real computer (Xie et al., 2024), or producing knowledge work that an expert grades (Patwardhan et al., 2025). Continuing tasks carry no terminal state, running without end in dynamic environments (Qian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026) and scoring an accumulated outcome that surfaces the failures long horizons produce, among them loss of coherence and an inability to turn experience into better decisions. Business operations provide natural continuing scenario with high-stakes, irreversible decisions, where compounding financial health tests sustained agent competence. Despite its promise, current benchmarks capture this environment only partially. While the Vending-Bench series (Backlund & Petersson, 2025; Andon Labs, 2026) simulates multi-round supplier negotiations, its reliance on mock data and prompt-based simulation yields highly stochastic supplier feedback that is vulnerable to manipulation. YC-Bench (He et al., 2026) runs deterministic startup year yet involves no supplier sourcing. Data-grounded retail benchmarks such as MerchantBench (Shi et al., 2026) and RetailBench (Zhang et al., 2026c) add real products and open code while dropping negotiation and adversarial dynamics altogether. Evidently, existing benchmarks either deviate from real-world market dynamics or rely on purely LLM-driven counterparts for multi-round negotiations, which introduces substantial sampling noise and ultimately compromises both the credibility and reproducibility of the evaluation. To address these, we introduce E-Commerce Bench, the first open-source benchmark that unifies deterministic supplier negotiation and customer sales modeling within real-world continuing business operation (Figure 3). Across simulated 365-day year, an agent can run up to four online stores concurrently, researching the market, negotiating for cost-effective goods, formulating sales strategies, and managing cash flow to maximize end-of-year total assets. Grounded in Taobao & Tmall data, the environment encompasses total of 6,886 products and 576 suppliers calibrated from empirical platform logs, while year-long calendar of promotional events, natural disasters, and supply-chain shocks continually shifts dynamic market demand. Critical market factors, such as baseline product costs and exact consumer demand, remain hidden, requiring the agent to continuously search, negotiate, and model market dynamics through dedicated e-commerce toolset provided by the benchmark. Meanwhile, the benchmark harness automatically manages the context window and offers persistent memory module (Packer et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023) to sustain year-long operational horizon. To ensure rigorous reproducibility, determinism governs both sides of the market. Customer purchases and returns follow fixed demand model that combines price elasticity, weekday, seasonality, scheduled promotions, market events, and store reputation, with its only randomness seeded from the episode so runs reproduce exactly. On the supply side, deterministic negotiation kernel fixes every pricing, concession, and accept/reject decision through explicit bargaining policies, while an LLM only renders them as dialogue. Roughly quarter of the suppliers turn adversarially fraudulent, on kernels that do not vary between runs. No sampling noise reaches the customers or the counterparts pricing and accept/reject decisions, so difference in outcome entirely belongs to the agent policy rather than to chance. Only the LLM renderers wording varies between runs (3.5.2). We evaluate 18 leading frontier and open-weight models along multi-dimensional metrics spanning negotiation quality, fraud avoidance, cash flow and solvency, operational efficiency, operations execution, and learning over the horizon, rather than by total assets alone. radar over the primary score and those six dimensions comes out visibly uneven, and six of the seven models it draws, one per vendor family, fall below the eighteen-model median on at least one axis (Figure 2). GPT-5.6 Sol grows its capital roughly 14-fold, yet ranks 16th of 18 on fraud avoidance and earns less from tool call than Fable5 does, while Claude Opus 4.7 leads both bargaining and fraud avoidance from mid-pack on profit. Among the ten open-weight entries, first place goes to our own Qwen3.8-Max-Preview at 4.2 times the initial balance, and four of the eighteen models slip into bankruptcy on part of their runs. Qwen3.8-Max-Preview is the strongest model in the field, improving over the year. Across 8,647 repeat purchases of the same item from the same honest supplier, 16 models show no clear sign of pushing the purchase price down as the year goes on, exposing critical deficiencies in their long-horizon experiential learning. We make three principal contributions. 1. We present E-Commerce Bench, realistic business environment grounded in Taobao & Tmall platform data, and the first open-source benchmark to combine deterministic counterpart negotiations, dynamic events, and concurrent multi-store management over year-long horizon. 2. We keep the economy deterministic on both sides of the market, with fixed demand model driving customer purchases and returns and deterministic negotiation kernel setting every pricing, concession, and accept/reject decision while an LLM only renders dialogue. The kernel extends the negotiation-partner design of TERMS-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026a) to repeated, cross-supplier bargaining. 3. We evaluate 18 models along multi-dimensional metrics, so one total-assets figure can no longer hide where model is weak. Reading six dimensions beside that total turns leaderboard into capability profile, and the profiles come out sharply divergent, the best earner being neither the best negotiator nor the efficient operator. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews long-horizon agentic benchmarks and positions E-Commerce Bench among them. Section 3 details the benchmark, covering its four-layer architecture, the deterministic negotiation kernel, the real-data economy, and the evaluation metrics. Section 4 reports results for the 18 models on every measured dimension, together with an error analysis of recurring failure modes. sections.title: 2.1 Episodic Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
sections.content: Long-horizon agentic benchmarks are divided by whether run carries terminal state (Sutton & Barto, 2018). Episodic benchmarks define one, setting goal and rewarding the multi-step execution that reaches it. Work-value benchmarks grade an economically meaningful deliverable, GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2025) scoring knowledge work against expert judgment and TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2025) setting simulated employees tasks inside software firm. Environment-grounded benchmarks stretch the horizon through real software, SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) resolving GitHub issue against its own tests and OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) driving real operating system over many GUI steps. Exploration-driven benchmarks probe reasoning further still, UltraHorizon (Luo et al., 2025) hiding the rules of partially observable world and EdgeBench (Zhu et al., 2026) learning from one environment for 12 to 72 hours at time. However long these tasks run, each ends the moment its goal is met, reducing evaluation solely to the quality of the final deliverable. Consequently, this setup fails to assess an agents ability in dynamic environments to track dependencies across hundreds of sub-tasks, recover from unexpected failures, or leverage accumulated history to optimize future actions. 2.2 Continuing Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks Continuing tasks carry no terminal state, so the agent acts indefinitely and earns an accumulated score. The shape recurs across trading live portfolio for cumulative return (Qian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026) and self-evolving agents that grow skill library (Wang et al., 2023) or rewrite their own code (Zhang et al., 2026b). The setting E-Commerce Bench belongs to is business-operation simulation, where the agent runs going concern and is judged by its accumulated balance. Vending-Bench (Backlund & Petersson, 2025) established the line, running one vending machine over roughly two thousand messages and exposing failures of long-term coherence, with LLM-generated supplier replies that leave runs stochastic. VendingBench 2 (Andon Labs, 2026) extends it to full year and adds adversarial suppliers, still LLM-driven. YC-Bench (He et al., 2026) runs deterministic startup year against rule-based clients but no supplier negotiation. Two benchmarks are grounded in real data, MerchantBench (Shi et al., 2026) over 365 days of seller-side operation with suppliers arriving as stochastic events, and RetailBench (Zhang et al., 2026c) over 180 supermarket days against privileged oracle. Neither offers negotiation or adversarial suppliers, and RetailBench lists strategic supplier behavior and multi-store coordination among the things it leaves out. Table 1 contrasts the five. The Vending-Bench line couples negotiation with adversarial suppliers in its sequel, but only through sampled LLM parties and without an open, real-data economy, while the data-grounded retail pair buys reproducibility by giving those dynamics up. E-Commerce Bench holds all six properties at once, and no other entry pairs negotiating counterpart with reproducible supplier economics. TERMS-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026a) sits outside the business-operation line, diagnosing bilateral price bargaining against rule-based counterpart over sampled regimes rather than data-grounded cost floors, so it supplies scripted opponent but no economy for the resulting deals to act on. Our market is deterministic on both sides, fixed demand model driving customers while deterministic negotiation kernel adapts that counterpart design to set every pricing and accept/reject decision, leaving an LLM only the dialogue rendering. 6 Figure 3: Overview of E-Commerce Bench. The agent works through four layers. An agent loop layer carries turn-based control, context management, and persistent memory, and tool layer holds the 18 e-commerce tools. Under both sits deterministic environment layer, the sales-and-economy engine beside the two-layer negotiation engine, computing over data layer derived from real e-commerce platform.

sections.title: 3 E-Commerce Bench
sections.content: 3.1 Overview E-Commerce Bench hands the agent merchant account, 100,000, and the 2026 calendar year on simulated Chinese online marketplace. The job is to end the year with as much money as possible. The agent researches which store types and categories carry demand, bargains suppliers down, buys inventory and publishes it to one of at most four stores. From there it prices the goods, reads yesterdays sales, ships orders, absorbs the returns, and withdraws settled revenue before the next operating charge lands. To evaluate the strategies driving the year-end profit, we independently score six core capabilities: negotiation quality, fraud avoidance, cash flow and solvency, operational efficiency, operational execution, and long-horizon learning (3.7). Next, we introduce the four layers of E-Commerce Bench in detail. 3.2 Agent Loop Layer Three mechanisms sit between the model and the environment. The turn loop (Figure 4) bounds what one model call can do, and charges simulated minutes for every tool it uses. Every turn adds its tool traffic to the message list, and year of calls overruns the window many times, so the context editor evicts the oldest turns first. The window is not the real limit either, since long contexts degrade well before they overflow (Liu et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024). Because evicted text leaves nothing behind, the agent also gets persistent memory system beyond the reach of any eviction pass. 7 Figure 4: The agent loop layer. One model call produces batch of tool calls; the batch runs in order, and timed tool advances the simulated clock inside its own call. The daily settlement fires whenever the clock reaches the next 08:00, whether timed tool carried it there or the agent asked to skip to tomorrow. Tools read and write the hidden environment state, and the settlement writes back to it as well, posting that days fees, sales, and returns. The days news and any notices are appended to the tool responses. The transcript is left alone until it passes 120,000 tokens, and only then are its oldest groups dropped. 3.2.1 Turn-Based Loop and Simulated Time Within single turn, the model can request several tools, which then run one by one in the order given. Turns therefore range from single balance check to batch of dozen tools. An episode runs to cap of 4,000 turns (4.1), or ends early once the model goes three turns without calling tool. Every tool but the day jump costs simulated minutes: 10 for balance check and 60 for opening store (Table 3 in Appendix A), spent out of 600-minute day that runs from 08:00 to 18:00. Looking something up draws on the same clock as acting on it. message costs 30 minutes whether it goes to one supplier or to ten, so twenty of them fill day. Once the clock passes 18:00, it jumps to 08:00 the next morning, which wait_for_next_day also does on request, costing no minutes but forfeiting the rest of the day. Every jump runs the same fixed sequence, charging operating and storage costs, turning the previous days demand into orders, cancelling shipments that missed their two-day deadline, settling matured escrow, delivering arriving purchase orders, and updating reputation (3.4). What the agent gets back after advancing to the next day is four thin signals: the days news feed, reminder once the bank balance no longer covers the days operating cost, the current time, and warning about token usage (Appendix A). Anything more precise costs tool call and the minutes that come with it. 3.2.2 Context Management single tokenizer counts each models context to ensure all of them work against the same 128,000-token budget. context eviction is triggered whenever the count reaches 120,000 tokens, taking 60,000 as its release target. Whole tool-call groups go, an assistant message and every tool response after it, oldest first (Figure 5). The system message, the first user turn, and the two newest groups are spared. The agent is told the policy verbatim, thresholds included, so preserving what matters in its memory is choice it can make. Across the 90 evaluation episodes of 4, 1,495 evictions ran. How much history model loses scales with its total tool traffic, the turns it takes times what each turn drags in, and the two factors trade off. Claude Opus 4.7 finishes the year in 432 turns and has about four windows worth of transcript discarded along the way, while Gemini 3.5 Flash takes 2,628 turns and loses nearly nineteen windows worth. Turns alone do not settle it. Kimi K2.6 takes 1,017 turns and loses the same three and half windows as Claude Opus 4.7 at 432 turns, because it drags in 431 tokens turn against Opus 4.7s 1,058, and GPT-5.5 loses 28 windows in half Gemini 3.5 Flashs turns at 2,759 turn. Figure 5: How eviction works. group is what the editor removes as unit: one model reply together with every tool result that reply produced, so turn that called six tools is still one group, and about fifty groups fill the window. pass fires only once group pushes the count past 120,000 tokens, then drops whole groups, oldest first, until 60,000 tokens are released or the clearable groups run out. The system message, the first user turn and the two newest groups are kept.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Persistent Agentic Memory
sections.content: The memory store is list of notes the agent keeps in the environment rather than in its own messages, so eviction never touches it. The store holds at most 20 entries, each title and its content. The agent fully curates the store itselfcreating, updating, and pruning entries as needed (Shinn et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024; Sumers et al., 2024). Reading the store back is cheap in minutes yet expensive in tokens, since returned entries re-enter the context and become evictable like everything else. capable agent is thus incentivized to preserve high-value strategic knowledge, such as past settlement prices or identifying deceptive suppliers. 3.3 Tool Layer Eighteen tools cover merchants back office, in the seven groups Figure 3 draws, and Table 3 gives each one its minute cost and its effect. Every call but the day jump is billed in simulated minutes (3.2.1), which makes the tool list budget rather than menu. Checking the bank balance, the warehouse, and one stores status costs 10 minutes each. morning round of all three spends 30 minutes day, more than 18 working days across the year. Only chatbox can create purchase order, so every unit of inventory arrives through free-form text carrying fenced negotiate blocks (3.5.2). Routine mail, supplier offers, and fraudulent pitches (3.5.4) all cost the same 30 minutes through that one tool. 3.4 Sales and Economy Engine The sales and economy engine decides how much the agent sells and when it gets paid. Nothing about the market is sampled. fixed formula computes how many units customers buy each day, and money moves between accounts on fixed delays. The simulator still draws few random numbers, for instance when it turns fractional unit of demand into whole one, and those come from one seed shared by every run, so two episodes that take the same actions end the year with exactly the same money. 3.4.1 Multi-Store Setup An agent trades through stores it opens itself. Twelve store types are on offer, each covering different set of product categories, and at most four may trade at once, one per type (Appendix B.2). Opening one costs 500 and then 60 to 130 day to run, the harder types costing more. Closing store stops the daily charge, and stock left behind keeps accruing storage unless the agent liquidates it for 10% of purchase cost. Reopening later starts reputation over. market lookup grades categorys margin low, moderate, or high, while the price supplier will actually accept emerges only from bargaining (3.5). 3.4.2 Three-Account Deferred Settlement Money an agent has earned is not money it can spend. Cash sits in three places (Figure 6). The bank account pays every cost the moment it is incurred, purchase order in full the moment negotiation closes. sale pays nothing at first and only creates pending shipment. Once the agent ships it, the revenue enters escrow with the platforms commission already deducted. Nine days later that balance matures into the platform wallet, and only an explicit withdrawal moves it back to the bank account where costs are paid. refund is taken out of the escrow batch its sale belongs to, so return never touches spendable cash. One order shows the gap. 40-unit lot of mid-priced accessory costs 2,447 9 Figure 6: Three-account deferred settlement. (a) Costs leave the bank the day they are incurred, while revenue passes through escrow and the platform wallet first. (b) One 40-unit order bought at the opening quote and resold at reference, followed as cash for 16 days. the day it is placed and returns its first cash on day 16. Ten consecutive days closing with negative bank balance end the episode as bankrupt (Appendix C.7), so an agent selling at profit while leaving its revenue in the wallet can still fail (4). 3.4.3 Deterministic Multi-Factor Demand Model How many units are sold is product of named factors rather than random draw. Demand for one SKU on one day starts from what its category sells in store of that type. Six multipliers then act on that base: the response to the posted price, weekend uplift, the promotion the agent joined, the months seasonality, whatever the calendar holds that day, and the stores reputation. Two capacity terms trim the result, one for the category and one for the store, each ceiling on how much demand that category or that store can absorb in day. sections.title: 3.4.4 Fulfillment, Shipping Speed, and Returns
sections.content: Every sale has to be shipped, and how it ships is priced choice. Faster delivery costs more freight and brings back fewer returns, and bulkier parcel costs more again. An order left unshipped past its two-day deadline is canceled outright, the units going back to the warehouse unsold and the cancellation counting against reputation. Returns are decided when goods ship and arrive days later, so fulfillment decision costs money long after it is taken (Petersen & Kumar, 2009). Four channels set units return probability, its categorys natural rate, whether the supplier shipped defective stock, how far above reference the agent priced it, and the shipping speed chosen (Appendix C.4). defective unit carries return rate of at least 0.40 and at least double the natural rate, capped at 0.95. Pricing at 1.3 times reference multiplies the rate by 1.50, and slow shipping by further 1.30. Every arriving return refunds the customer out of escrow and puts the unit back in the warehouse on fresh storage clock. Two of the four channels answer to the agent, its pricing and its freight tier, so models return rate reads partly as management outcome rather than only as property of the catalog (3.7). 3.4.5 Reputation System stores reputation multiplies its demand directly (3.4.3), so service failures cost sales. Credit accrues when an order ships rather than when it sells, so an unshipped order earns nothing and draws the cancellation penalty as well. Returns and cancellations subtract from the same standing, weighted 0.6 and 1.0 (Resnick et al., 2000), so missed deadline costs more than change of mind. store pinned at the floor receives 15% of the demand it would receive at the top, and the capacity terms return part of that loss once they bind (Appendix C.3). 3.4.6 Dynamic Event System The calendar moves demand whether or not the agent is ready. Market events arrive on fixed dates, scaling demand per store type and stretching delivery lead times (Appendix B.3, Table 6 and Figure 15). Direction is rarely uniform, so storm that lifts food cuts fashion and footwear. News of an event reaches the agents feed as the event begins, while promotion is announced week ahead without its dates or its size. Joining reveals the size, and the years first sale is already running when its announcement lands. The boost from joining peaks at 30% discount, so deeper cut adds demand only through the price response while margin falls on every unit. Suppliers exit on count rather than date, each retiring after hidden number of filled orders, so counterpart whose floor the agent has learned can be gone by the next re-order. 3.4.7 Daily Settlement and Processing Lifecycle Costs are charged before any revenue is recognized, so every morning tests solvency at the days low point. Sales are then computed for the previous calendar date against the inventory and prices the agent left standing overnight, so the agent steers system that lags it by day. Refunds leave escrow before matured escrow settles, so return can empty the batch that was about to pay out. Appendix C.1 lists all thirteen steps with the state each one touches.

sections.title: 3.5 Deterministic Negotiation Engine
sections.content: The negotiation engine sets what the agent pays for stock. Every unit it sells has to be bought from named supplier, one chatbox message at time, at price the two of them argue over. Roughly quarter of the roster takes the money instead of earning it (3.5.4), so counterpart has to be chosen as well as bargained with.

sections.title: 3.5.1 Bargaining Policy Preliminaries
sections.content: Sourcing one SKU begins with message to one supplier and ends in price or in nothing. Neither side sees the others limit. supplier never reveals the floor below which it will not sell, so each purchase is bilateral bargaining problem under incomplete information (Harsanyi, 1967; Chatterjee & Samuelson, 1983; Rubinstein, 1982). One such cycle is session = (s, j, c), the c-th between supplier and SKU j. No rule closes session at fixed round. deadline scale sets the time pressure instead, and past its midpoint supplier can walk away from an offer under its floor (Appendix D.1). One pair from the evaluation fixes the scale. Ridge Express quotes single SKU at 149.81, and the agent resells against market reference of 199.75. Beneath both lies floor of 101.27 the agent never sees, leaving 98.48 for the two sides to divide. Figure 8 follows one such session offer by offer in panel (a), and the nine deals the pair produced across the year in panel (b). Two prices bracket what session can be worth. The agent resells against public market reference price vj (3.4), while supplier holds private floor cs j. Bargaining runs in the gap between the two, the zone of possible agreement (ZOPA), so deal at unit price pz for qz units hands the agent (vj pz) qz of it. How wide that gap is, how badly the supplier needs the sale and how hard it will push are drawn once and stay hidden. The agent bargains without knowing how much room it has. Sessions are divided by counterpart type, one term of the objective per side. Writing ZG for those concluded with the honest suppliers and ZB for those concluded with the fraudulent ones (3.5.4), the year-end asset goal of 3.1 becomes procurement objective. max π 1[fz = ] (vj(z) pz) qz 1[fz = ] ℓz . (2) zZG {z surplus extracted from honest suppliers } zZB {z losses paid to fraudulent suppliers } Here fz is the session outcome, disagreement worth nothing, and ℓz what fraudulent deal costs in the end, whether overpayment, fees, short shipment or defective stock. Two competencies follow, and they pull against each other. Winning surplus from an honest supplier takes firmness; refusing fraudulent one takes walking away, and the firmness that wins good price is also what produces impasse (Raiffa, 1982). Both are paid in the cash that sets the primary score. 3.5.2 Two-Layer Supplier Design An outcome difference says something about the agent only if every model met the same counterpart economics in every run. supplier played entirely by an LLM breaks that twice over. Sampling moves its prices from run to run, and it stays persuadable, so an eloquent enough agent can talk it below its own floor and turn the benchmark into jailbreaking contest. Every supplier therefore splits into two layers. Layer 1, the Deterministic Negotiation Kernel. Every price, concession and accept or walk-away decision comes from deterministic kernel rather than from model. The kernel builds on the counterpart policy of Zhang et al. (2026a), reimplemented independently in seller-only role and re-parameterized from the data layer (Appendix D). Acceptance and walk-away are stochastic (Baarslag et al., 2014), and latent cue carries sentiment and posture (Appendix D.1). Counter-offers answer the agents own concession speed rather than the clock (Faratin et al., 1998), so an agent that concedes fast meets firmer counterpart. Fast concession carries the same disadvantage in human bargaining (Tey et al., 2021). One kernel serves one (supplier, SKU) pair. Its reservation price and opening quote come from the data layer, so both are properties of the SKU rather than draws. Its seed makes an identical agent trajectory meet an identical supplier response (Appendix D.2). Two sources of run-to-run variance survive. The Layer 2 renderer is an LLM sampled at its providers default decoding, and the delivery days suppliers catalog advertises are drawn outside the episode seed, so they can move between runs. Prices and accept or walk decisions cannot move, but the narrative model reads to detect fraud does, so the fraud axis of 4.3.2 carries renderer sampling noise on top of policy sampling noise. Honest suppliers draw from six behavior templates. The templates differ in how sharply the kernel answers the agents concession speed and in how much its cues give away. Which supplier gets which is fixed in 12 Figure 8: Negotiation at two timescales, from real episodes, each panel on its own price axis and the cost floor hidden from the agent. (a) One session offer by offer, the agent bidding up and the kernel conceding down until the agent accepts its standing quote. (b) The same (supplier, SKU) pair all year, where that session ends run of near-floor deals and the price never recovers, the hatched wedge being the overpayment AnchorRegret averages. (c) Another agent instead pushes lower at nearly every restock. the released roster, so the difficulty mix is set rather than drawn per run (Appendix D.3). Neither the template nor the honest or fraudulent label is visible to the agent. Layer 2, the NPC renderer. second LLM turns each committed kernel decision into supplier chat. The renderer has to relay the exact price and decision and takes only tone from the kernels sentiment cue, which keeps the dialogue rich and economically inert. Compliance does not rest on that instruction. An accept is refused unless its price matches the kernels standing quote to within 0.005, so renderer that misstated price could never make it transaction (Appendix D.4). In the other direction, deterministic parser reads the agents own offer, accept and reject actions out of the same free-form message. One economic action travels in the prose instead, enrolment in suppliers membership program, which an intent classifier recognizes from the agents own words and bills at 1,000 (Appendix D.5). Prices carry no signal about fraud by design, so on the pre-deal class the narrative holds the decisive evidence, and no fixed template could mount it. Figure 20 prints one session end to end, every supplier line beside the kernel decision it had to relay. 3.5.3 Multi-Round, Cross-Supplier, Repeated Bargaining One session is usually the unit of evaluation in existing negotiation benchmarks, and the kernel as described so far governs exactly one. Across full year the game becomes repeated, which asks whether an agent turns what one encounter taught it about counterpart into better price at the next. Inferring private reservation value from past encounters (Baarslag et al., 2016) therefore becomes part of the task rather than an assumption. Closed deals are not re-surfaced, so an agent keeps its own price history or does without it. Once session over (s, j) concludes, the next offer on that pair opens fresh cycle under new kernel instance and new seed, carrying the same persistent type and reservation price. seller-side kernel never accepts below that reservation, so the best price won so far is an upper bound on cs that only tightens. The competence it rewards is to anchor each reopening at or below that historical best. Calling the rule optimal would go too far, since against pre-deal fraudulent counterpart the historical best tightens onto floor inflated on purpose (3.5.4). Learning runs on both sides of the table. Each suppliers deal history goes into its prompt, so suppliers remember what they sold before. Several honest suppliers serve every category alongside few fraudulent ones, so the agent can also arbitrate across counterparts, probing one suppliers floor and holding it as an outside option against another. Single-session skill and year-long accumulation then separate cleanly, the first measured in per-session surplus, the second in how fast the price for repeatedly sourced SKU walks down toward the floor (3.5.5). Every session costs twice over besides. Bargaining spends minutes out of the working day (3.2.1), and an agreement spends cash out of bank balance that refills only when escrow settles (3.4.2). session excellent in surplus terms can still be the wrong one to have opened.

sections.title: 3.5.4 Adversarial Supplier Fraud
sections.content: Of the 576 suppliers on the roster, 152 are fraudulent. Each runs the hardball kernel preset under one of five scripted scam overlays that the renderer performs. The five split into two classes by when the damage lands (Appendix D.5). No single observation gives fraudulent counterpart away. Opening quotes are uninformative by construction (3.5.2), and the behavior family stays latent and is shared with honest suppliers. What does separate the two populations is the rate of concession, since fraudulent kernels hold out longer than the hardest honest preset. That signal lives only in the shape of multi-round exchange, so an agent that accepts early gives up its one bargaining-side cue and has to read the narrative instead. Pre-deal scams make their money inside the negotiation. Their kernels carry reservation price inflated toward 1.5 the honest cost floor, so any deal overpays what an honest competitor would have charged. The inflated floor still sits inside the range an honest supplier might quote, so only the narrative gives it away, offering membership fees, discounts that never arrive, or manufactured urgency. Post-deal scams keep the honest cost floor and quote from that same range, then defect at fulfillment. short delivery brings 60% to 70% of the quantity paid for, and defective stock returns at 0.40 or double the SKUs natural rate, whichever is higher, capped at 0.95 (3.4). The defective rate is blended across the SKUs pooled stock, so interleaving honest and fraudulent deliveries dilutes the evidence and no observed return rate points back to culprit. Scoring therefore counts the money actually lost to these counterparts rather than judging intent (3.5.5), which keeps the axis on the cash of Equation (2).

sections.title: 3.5.5 Negotiation Metrics
sections.content: Both terms of Equation (2) are scored as the fraction of the bargaining range an agent captures, standard practice in automated negotiation (Raiffa, 1982; Baarslag et al., 2013). The metrics build on the surplus efficiency of Zhang et al. (2026a), re-based from sampled ZOPA geometry onto data-grounded floors, and Appendix E.1 carries every formal definition. Agreement is close to universal on the honest sessions model concludes, so CSE+ carries the headline, the share of pairs bargaining range that closed deal captures. Beside it %Oracle compares the same surplus against closing every honest deal at the suppliers floor, and the agreement rate stays in Appendix E.1. Neither headline metric weights deal by quantity, and both are rates over session set the agent chose itself, so they measure per-deal bargaining skill rather than procurement cash saved. Two models compare on them only if their portfolios carry similar bargaining ranges, which 4.3.1 checks by reporting deal volume beside the rate. Conclusion is the operative word. session abandoned mid-bargain enters no denominator and costs nothing in any of the three metrics, so 4.3.1 reports abandonment counts beside them rather than folding them into rate. Fraud avoidance is reported as BadSpend% rather than as an agreement rate over fraudulent sessions, because the agent also chooses whom to contact at all. session-rate denominator would reward never looking, and cash is in any case the quantity scam actually costs. Sequential price discipline Over 365 days, the same supplier is asked for the same SKU many times, which raises question no session-level metric answers. Does an agents next order benefit from the price it already won? Holding an anchor like that has documented value in human bargaining (Petrowsky et al., 2025). The measure looks at every honest (supplier, SKU) pair traded more than once. Each agreed price is expressed as its position πz inside that pairs bargaining range, then scored after the first deal against the best the agent had already won there. AnchorRegret averages the resulting overpayment. AnchorRatio divides that average by null which holds each pairs prices fixed and reshuffles only the order they arrived in. Significance travels separately in the permutation z-score zanchor. The null assumes pairs cycles are equally hard, and that assumption is checkable rather than asserted. Two of the three quantities that set that difficulty are constants of the SKU, and the archive records the cost floor and the nominal wholesale reference unchanged across all 8,647 re-orders. The quote the kernel actually opens with is redrawn each cycle and the archive does not keep it, so rising πz is read against fixed floor rather than against fixed opening. The measure reports an outcome and not its cause, and 4.3.6 takes up which mechanism produces it. Figure 8 shows both outcomes on real trajectories, one agent giving back price it had already won while another walks its price down the range all year. Three limits bound the scope. Only honest pairs count, since pre-deal fraudulent floor is inflated by construction (3.5.4). Each re-order counts equally regardless of order size, so the measure captures per-unit discipline and not its cash consequence. No observations come from an episode that ends early. 3.6 Data Layer Every number E-Commerce Bench runs on comes from real e-commerce platform, either desensitized straight off it or synthesized by hand against an analysis of its data logs, the supplier price floors of 3.5 and the demand parameters of 3.4 among them.

sections.title: 3.6.1 Catalog and Suppliers
sections.content: The environment ships 6,886 products in 60 categories, served by 576 suppliers, 424 of them honest and 152 fraudulent. The 12 store types span 9 categories down to 1, and the calendar fixes 10 market events and 8 promotions. Desensitization maps the products, the categories, the per-category return-rate tiers, the monthly-sales bands and the holiday calendar straight off real e-commerce platform. Synthesis from real logs supplies the rest, namely the four price-elasticity families, seasonality curves, reputation parameters and supplier attributes. Promotion names are fictional, since model that recognizes Chinas largest shopping festival could price from memory rather than from evidence (Zhu et al., 2025). Fraud reaches every product line rather than concentrating in few. Each supplier serves exactly one category, no category holds fewer than 7 honest and 2 fraudulent, and coverage stays flat across catalog depth (Figure 13d). Every fraudulent one runs scam of 3.5.4. The supplier list is fixed at release rather than redrawn per episode, and Appendix lists all 60 categories with their parameters.

sections.title: 3.6.2 Systematic Information Asymmetry
sections.content: An agent sees the catalog and the outcomes of its own actions, never the demand and cost-floor parameters that decide what an action is worth. market lookup answers at one of three levels: the coarsest naming every store type and the finest one categorys sales band  (Table 3)  , each substituting label for the quantity behind it. profit-potential grade replaces demand capacity, margin class the wholesale ratio, and sentence about returns the per-SKU rate. Supplier lookup withholds most, naming no type and ranking nothing (3.5.2). Pre-deal scams show in the narrative from the opening quote (3.5.4). Post-deal ones are written to read like ordinary suppliers, so only the goods that arrive expose them, and the cash has left by then. Table 7 in Appendix sets each observable against the quantity it withholds and prices the discovery. Portfolio decisions therefore rest on inference, and hidden parameters differ widely in how fast they can be learned. The best price already won from supplier bounds its floor from above (3.5.3), and SKUs natural return rate becomes readable once its stock has moved. An elasticity parameter stays hidden all year, since four unprinted factors multiply the same observation. store types earning ceiling shows only after one has been operated for year. Exploration and operation both cost time (3.2), so the year rewards allocating discovery rather than exhausting it. 3.7 Evaluation and Metrics The primary score is end-of-year total assets, the sum of the bank account, the platform wallet, and unsettled escrow, reported as the asset multiplier over the 100,000 opening stake. Bankruptcy ends run before the horizon (3.4.2). Truncated runs enter the average rather than being dropped, so five-run mean can mix them with full years. Six capabilities are measured around the year-end assets: (1) Bargaining is scored on how far down the agent pushes price. CSE+ ranks negotiation quality, how much of the distance from the public reference price down to the suppliers cost floor closed honest deal covers, where 1 means buying at the floor and 0 means paying the reference price, averaged over sessions with no weight for order size. Recorded around it are SE+, %Oracle, AGR+, rounds to deal, deals closed, and both surplus and spending broken out by the suppliers behavior template (E.1). (2) Fraud avoidance follows the cash rather than the conversation. Ranking runs on BadSpend%, the share of order spending that cleared into fraudulent suppliers account, low being the better direction. We also record the fraud agreement rate (the percentage of fraudulent sessions ending in deal), alongside diagnostics covering losses across the five scams, membership fees paid, and fraudulent suppliers contacted or ordered from (E.2). (3) Solvency is judged by how much of its own best position year gave back. Peak drawdown over peak total assets ranks cash flow and solvency, since the archive records that fall in absolute , and business ten times the size books ten times the fall for the same discipline. The unnormalized fall, the bankrupt runs, the overdrawn days, the deepest bank balance, the idle platform wallet, and the largest warehouse held round out the dimension (E.3). (4) Operational efficiency prices year of profit against the calls that produced it. Mean profit over mean tool calls orders the models. Sitting next to it are the call count, its split over eight activity bands, the turns, the eviction passes the transcript needed, and the memory-store traffic (E.4). (5) Operations execution is ranked by the controllable return ratethe excess returns driven by the models pricing above the baseline (accrued at dispatch; negative for discounted prices), excluding fraud-induced defects. Supporting diagnostics include realized returns, refund and freight losses, on-time delivery rates, orders lost to the two-day deadline, tier mix, and store counts (E.5). (6) Learning is read from what an agent does every time after the first that it buys the same item from the same supplier, which over year is usually several times. AnchorRatio ranks learning over the horizon by measuring how much each repeat order overpays against the cheapest that agent had yet paid that supplier for that item. sections.title: 4 Experimental Results
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Eighteen models ran the 365-day task, eight proprietary and ten open-weight by our own assignment, ranked within tier by mean total assets  (Table 10)  . Each model received five independent episodes, 90 in all, under one fixed world. Requests use each providers default settings, with no temperature or top_p sent and thinking force-enabled wherever family exposes it  (Table 10)  . Five episodes is small sample, so every mean in Table 2 is printed with its standard deviation (Miller, 2024; Kapoor et al., 2025). Otherwise, all models shared the same 18 tools  (Table 3)  , context window and group-wise eviction (3.2.2), and the memory store outside it (3.2.3). The longest episode took 3,599 turns of the 4,000 allowed, and all 90 ended on the simulated calendar or in bankruptcy rather than on that cap. One renderer voices every supplier for every model, so wording varies between episodes while the economics it relays cannot (3.5.2). Scoring reduces the year to one number, the asset multiplier, end-of-year total assets over the 100,000 stake (Appendix E). bankrupt episode stops on the tenth consecutive negative bank day and still enters the average. 4.2 Overall Performance Starting from the same stake in the same simulated year, the models finish orders of magnitude apart. factor of 1,264 separates GPT-5.6 Sol at the top from Qwen3.5-Plus at the bottom (Table 2, Figure 1). The environment is deterministic given the action sequence (4.1), so that range belongs to the agents rather than to resampled demand. Proprietary systems take the top four places  (Table 2)  . Qwen3.8-Max-Preview leads the open-weight tier and places fifth overall. Inside the Qwen family each release earns more than the one before it, and Qwen3.8-Max-Preview earns the most. The 3.6 to 3.7 step is worth noting, since Qwen3.7-Max swings from 6,290 to 358,790 across its five years, and its worst year finishes below every Qwen3.6-Plus year. Strong models go bankrupt too. Ten of the ninety episodes ended insolvent, six of them under closed-source models. GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen3.5-Plus account for all ten, and the same four surrender more than half of peak total assets (4.3.3). Ordering by assets recovers only part of the skill behind it (Figure 2). Section 4.3 takes the axes one at time, and Appendix carries the per-model table of every dimension. 16 Figure 9: Capability profiles for six of the 18 models. The primary score and the six dimensions of this section run clockwise from the top, profit as mean end-of-year total assets, negotiation as CSE+, fraud avoidance as BadSpend%, solvency as peak drawdown over peak total assets, efficiency as profit per tool call, execution as the controllable return rate and learning as AnchorRatio. Fraud avoidance, solvency, execution and learning are sign-flipped so that higher is better on every axis. Each axis is min-max normalized over the 18 model means, so 1 marks the best mean and 0 the worst, with whiskers over the five episodes and dashed polygon at the median. Efficiency carries no episode spread, being ratio of 5-run means, and the archived AnchorRatio spread is population std over varying number of episodes, so the learning axis draws no whisker either. No profile fills the polygon. 4.3 Multi-Dimensional Analysis Six dimensions pull the year apart, each ranked by one recorded measure and defined in 3.7, with the formulas, field names, and caveats in one appendix subsection per dimension (E.1 to E.6). Figure 9 sets the primary score beside the six axes for six models, and Appendix F.8 carries all 18. 4.3.1 Negotiation Quality No model bargains prices down to the suppliers cost floor. Claude Opus 4.7 keeps the most of each bargaining range at 0.811 and Kimi K2.6 the least at 0.596, with the per-model values in Table 11. Accepting the opening quote already scores 0.50, so the field lands 0.10 to 0.31 above what taking the first offer would have cost it (Appendix D.2). Which counterpart model draws matters less than which model it is, since the field spreads 0.051 across the six behavior templates against 0.204 across models, though the per-model ordering inside column still moves by as much as thirteen places (Figure 23). Agreement rates sit at the top of their scale and separate nobody. Of the 12,060 concluded honest sessions, 73 end without deal, and 72 of those are the agents own rejection rather than supplier walking away. Every model settles at least 96% of the honest sessions it concludes, so the ranking rests on how much deal captures rather than on how often one happens (Appendix E.1). The rate also leaves out the 10.9% of sessions model opened mid-year and never came back to. Agents buy least from the counterparts that concede least. The hardest of the six honest behavior templates (Appendix D.3) covers 48 of the 424 honest names on the supplier list, and those 48 take 4.8% of the 55.1M of honest procurement, against at least 14% for each of the five easier ones (Figure 24). Buying the same item from the same honest supplier again costs more than reshuffle of the prices already won would have, for 16 of the 18 models, 17 and 4.3.6 takes that up with the rest of the years trends.

sections.title: 4.3.2 Fraud Avoidance
sections.content: Every model sends part of its procurement budget to suppliers that defraud it. Spending on them spans more than 160-fold, cleanest at Claude Opus 4.7 and heaviest at Qwen3.5-Plus (Figure 25), and none spends as though it never screened. BadSpend% counts money rather than refusals (E.2), unlike refusal rate on scripted solicitations (Yang et al., 2025), so declining an offer the agent never sought earns no credit. share and sum of money rank the models differently, because procurement budgets differ as widely as the shares do. Qwen3.5-Plus gives up the largest share, yet GPT-5.6 Sol hands over fifty times the cash on smaller one  (Table 12)  . Both readings rest on handful of orders, and across five episodes the standard deviation of the share exceeds its own mean for 15 of the 18 models. Losing money to fraud does not cost model its year. The cleanest buyer finishes mid-pack on assets and the profit leader is 16th of 18 on BadSpend% (4.2), because pre-deal scam inflates price that still sits inside the honest range and post-deal scam delivers most of the goods (3.5.4). Most of the money disappears after deal is signed. Defective lots take 53.4% of everything reaching fraudulent suppliers and short shipments the next largest slice (Figure 25), while membership-fee scams almost never land, three payments in the whole evaluation. Models separate when they order, not when they choose whom to approach. Fraudulent suppliers take close to their share of the supplier list in every models outreach (3.5.2), and what differs is how often an approach becomes an order, from 4.0% for Claude Opus 4.7 to 31.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol (Figure 26, Appendix F.3). negotiation that reaches its end almost always closes deal (4.3.1), so the gap lies in the approaches model abandons. 4.3.3 Cash Flow and Solvency Money leaves the bank account weeks before it returns. Revenue waits nine days in escrow, then waits again for withdrawal (3.4.2). No episode sees cash in the wallet before day 15, and 49 of the 90 bottom out in January. Two GPT-5.5 episodes went bankrupt on day 17, before single yuan of revenue had settled. Returns claw more money back out of escrow (4.3.5). fall recorded in yuan grows with the balance at risk, and the largest of the field belongs to GPT-5.6 Sol, which also earned the most (Appendix E.3). Dividing each fall by the peak total assets of its own episode separates the field on risk, and the five models that surrendered more than half of peak include all four that ever went bankrupt (Figure 27a, Table 13). Running the bank account below zero was rare and usually fatal. Seventeen of the 90 episodes went negative at morning check across 177 such days, and ten of them went bankrupt. run ends only after ten consecutive overdrawn mornings, so one Claude Opus 4.6 episode absorbed fifteen scattered overdrafts and survived. On 66 of those days the wallet already held the shortfall (Figure 27b). No tool reports the streak (3.2), so an agent cannot count the mornings it has failed. large cash buffer buys survival and caps growth. Three models kept the bank above 15,000 in every episode and finished sixth, tenth and eleventh, while the two biggest earners held the thinnest average buffers of the fourteen solvent models. Qwen3.8-Max-Preview leads the open-weight field on mid-field buffer, its bank above zero all year. 4.3.4 Operational Efficiency Fable5 earns more from tool call than the leader does. Sitting second on total assets, it turns 479 of profit out of each call against GPT-5.6 Sols 363, on 59.9% fewer calls  (Table 14)  . Three models finish under their opening stake, so their calls average loss over the year, 92 call at the worst. No fee inside the economy charges for call, so the bill falls on whoever deploys the agent and the score stays blind to it (Kapoor et al., 2025). The Berkeley function-calling leaderboard reports that bill directly, printing dollar cost and latency beside accuracy (Patil et al., 2025). Where the calls go describes policy better than their number does (Figure 10b). Shipping, advancing the day, withdrawing settled revenue and publishing inventory absorb 71.8% of all 18 models calls, daily loop rather than plan. Reading state back takes another 14.7% and supplier conversation 6.0%, so the one channel that can change what an item costs draws less than fifteenth of the effort. Pricing barely registers in the call budget. One call can revise many prices at once, yet 0.66% of all calls do so. Nine of the 18 models average under three such calls year, leaving their listed prices to stand while season, promotion and reputation move demand underneath them. The memory store draws almost no traffic. Notes the eviction pass cannot reach (3.2.3) take 2.1% of the fields calls. Claude Opus 4.8 gives it the largest share of its own budget, 4.7% at 69.6 calls year against 20 slots, while GPT-5.5 makes the most calls outright at 135.2 and Qwen3.5-Plus wrote to it in none of its five episodes. Twenty notes revised few dozen times is what year of trading leaves behind. Figure 10: (a) Profit per tool call for the 18 models, best first, mean total assets less the 100,000 stake divided by mean tool calls per episode. Bankrupt episodes are pooled into both means, and the three models that finish under the stake sit left of zero. (b) Where six models spent their calls, over eight groups of the 18 tools, scaled within each model. 4.3.5 Operations Execution The controllable return rate counts the percentage points models own pricing adds above the natural rate of the goods it chose to sell, and it is the one return channel this axis charges to the agent. The points run from 0.05 for Qwen3.7-Max to 5.88 for Qwen3.5-Plus  (Table 15)  . The natural rate underneath is larger, 5.31 to 21.25 points, and it follows what model chose to sell rather than how it priced. Twenty-six of the 90 episodes carry negative rate, priced under the reference. Added returns are worth buying when the price that causes them pays for them. GPT-5.6 Sol books 4.46 points and the years largest refund bill, 1.62M, and finishes first on assets. Qwen3.5-Plus adds more return points than any other model and finishes last. Freight speed is chosen once and left alone. The archive holds 92,182 fast dispatches beside 171,642 standard and exactly one slow, and 72 of the 88 episodes that sold anything put at least 98% of shipments in one tier. Fast doubles the freight bill and cuts the return draw by quarter, yet nine models swing over 30 points in fast share between their own episodes, so the tier reads as sampling, not policy. Store openings order nothing. Cumulative openings run from 3.0 for two Qwen models to 9.0 for GPT-5.6 Sol, each charging the 500 setup fee again and restarting reopened types reputation at the floor. GLM 5.2 (high) opened exactly four every episode and placed sixth, while Gemini 3.5 Flash opened 13 in one episode and placed twelfth, and neither is profitable habit. 4.3.6 Learning over the Horizon Two of the 18 models pay less on repeat order than reshuffling of the prices they already won from that supplier would have cost. Qwen3.8-Max-Preview scores 0.834 on AnchorRatio and Gemini 3.5 Flash 0.918, where 1.0 means an agents price ordering is indistinguishable from random ordering of its own prices. The field median is 1.369, and Qwen3.5-Plus reaches 1.860  (Table 16)  . Fifteen models miss their own permutation null by more than two standard deviations in the expensive direction, which is what an unrevised anchor on an early price produces (Lou & Sun, 2026). GPT-5.5 contributes three episodes instead of five; its two bankrupt runs never buy the same item twice from the same supplier. second reading of the same year runs the same way, with sixteen of the 18 models capturing less surplus in the Figure 11: One bankruptcy episode day by day, Qwen3.5-Plus episode 0. Total assets and bank balance are on the left axis, warehouse stock on the right, and the shaded band marks the days the bank balance stayed negative. second half of an episode than in the first. The surplus half-lift splits an episodes honest sessions at the median day and differences the two means (E.6). Three mechanisms would hold that surplus trend flat, and the evaluation separates none of them. Eviction destroys the tool result that carried price already won (3.2.2). The memory store that survives eviction is barely used (4.3.4). And no gradient reaches inside an episode, so improvement must come from an agent reasoning over its own record (Shinn et al., 2023). Qwen3.8-Max-Preview moves against the field, alone holding positive per-day surplus trend and alone beating its own shuffled prices by more than two standard deviations. Supplier choice drifts as well. Fraudulent suppliers take larger share of concluded sessions late in the year than early for 17 of the 18 models, so what moves over the horizon moves the wrong way. 4.4 Error Analysis The six axes rank models without locating the mistake, since one payment to supplier that cheats surfaces as fraudulent spend and again as deeper fall from peak assets. Ten recurring patterns therefore get one detection rule each, with mechanisms and counts in Table 18 and Figure 30 of Appendix G.5. Bankruptcy alone destroys the stake (4.3.3). Inventory bought and never sold is the road there. One Qwen3.5-Plus episode fills four stores in January, never sells its way out, and ends in May (Figure 11). Fraudulent suppliers charge for value they never deliver, inflating prices before goods move and shipping short afterwards. second order with the same supplier is where most of the money goes: 943 of the 1,141 agreements struck with fraudulent suppliers sit in supplier-item pair dealt with twice or more (4.3.2, Appendix E.1). No message names the supplier behind bad lot, so the loss lands in the balance instead of arriving as signal. Money lost in bargaining is small per deal and never fatal. Honest deals rarely close half the range available below, and the giveaway is the opening quote accepted unimproved (4.3.1). Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.5 Flash and Fable5 never accept one and are the top three on CSE+, Kimi K2.6 most often and last. Research gets re-derived instead of remembered. Of 2,180 catalog and supplier queries, 746 repeat arguments already issued that episode. The repeats cost 7,460 simulated minutes, 83 an episode against 219,000-minute year, and sit beside little-used memory store (4.3.6). Nothing in the economy charges for asking twice. The two-day shipping deadline binds only at the edges of the year. Cancellations cluster in the first fortnight and again in the final two weeks, where the agent has either not started shipping or has stopped (4.3.5). Three patterns often blamed for long-horizon failure do not survive the data. Store churn does not separate the field (4.3.5). Models that sign up for more promotions end richer, so event neglect explains nothing. Late-year collapse holds only in part, growth dropping after the first quarter at paired = 3.95 and the closing window flat rather than recovering. Failure patterns spread across the whole field rather than concentrating in the weakest models. Every model trips at least five rules, Gemini 3.1 Pro all ten, and tripping fewer of them does not make model richer. The cleanest profiles belong to the best bargainers, not the richest, so the field reads as strong in patches and coordinated nowhere (transcripts in Appendix G).

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce E-Commerce Bench, long-horizon benchmark in which an agent runs an online retail business for simulated 365-day year. The benchmark is built in four parts. An agent loop drives one model call at time and keeps year of tool traffic inside the context window, with persistent memory beside it. Eighteen tools cover the merchants job, from market research and supplier chat to pricing, shipping, and cash withdrawal. deterministic environment decides what customers buy and how suppliers bargain, computing over products, suppliers, and calendar taken from real e-commerce platform. Purchases and returns follow fixed demand model, and deterministic negotiation kernel makes every supplier price, concession, and accept/reject decision while an LLM only turns those decisions into dialogue. Eighteen frontier and open-weight models each ran the year five times, scored on end-of-year total assets and on six capabilities behind that number (3.7). No model is strong on all seven. GPT-5.6 Sol earns the most, turning the 100,000 stake into roughly 14 times as much, yet it ranks 16th of 18 on fraud avoidance and earns less per tool call than Fable5. Claude Opus 4.7 bargains best and avoids fraud best while finishing mid-pack on money, and Qwen3.8-Max-Preview leads the open-weight models at 4.2 times the stake. Four models go bankrupt in part of their runs, two GPT-5.5 episodes as early as day 17, before any revenue had settled (4.3.3). Beyond the retail domain, E-Commerce Bench offers foundational blueprint for next-generation agent evaluation. By proving that deterministic kernel control eliminates evaluation noise in complex multi-party interactions, and that multi-dimensional diagnostics are indispensable for catching diverse failure modes, we provide the methodology needed to push agent benchmarks into ever-longer horizons.

sections.content: A model sees the environment only through tool schemas and tool replies. Nothing else is sent to it, so every notice the environment has to deliver rides inside reply. The price list comes first, then the format of reply, then the eviction algorithm that holds year of transcript inside 128,000-token window. Sections 3.2 and 3.3 give the outline, and Table 3 the price list. Prompts are reproduced separately in Appendix H, and the eviction schematic with Section 3.2.2. A.1 The Interface Contract Every tool call comes back as single string. Structured results arrive as JSON, plain text unchanged. Extra notices sit inside that JSON rather than after its closing brace, so the reply still parses. Day-scoped notices attach to the day-advance result when the batch holds one and to the last response otherwise, so news is never blamed on an unrelated earlier call. The morning pass reports far less to the agent than it computes. Of the 17 fields it assembles, at most three reach the agent, the date, the day index and the news feed. Across the 90 archived episodes the channel carried 8,301 items, 6,722 of them deliveries at one aggregated line per day. The first carries the day notice, the second low-balance reminder, and both close with the token gauge that sits outside the JSON. The second run went bankrupt. A.2 Loop Control and Context Editing Token counts come from local tokenizer rather than the providers own report, and cover the text, the tool calls and the reasoning trace of each message. Opaque artifacts such as replayed encrypted reasoning items are excluded, as are the tool schemas held outside the budget (3.2.2). The system prompt quotes the model the 120,000-token threshold, the 60,000-token release floor and the two protected groups. One pass proceeds as follows. 1. Sum the counts of every message not already marked cleared. Below that ceiling the pass emits the usage string and frees nothing. 2. Scan for groups from the third message onward, leaving the system message and the first user turn permanently out of reach. group opens at an assistant message carrying tool calls and closes after the last consecutive tool response behind it. 3. Set aside the two most recent groups not yet cleared. With two or fewer active groups the pass clears nothing at all, so history made of few very large groups can sit above the ceiling indefinitely. 4. Take the release target as the larger of that floor and the current overshoot past the ceiling. 5. Walk the clearable groups oldest first, marking each cleared and accumulating its count, and stop at the first group that meets the target. 6. Rebuild the request from the surviving messages, skipping cleared entries entirely (3.2.2). Whether pass ever fires depends on how model spends the window, and Figure 12 counts the passes of each of the 90 episodes. Two kinds of message can never be evicted, an assistant turn of plain text and the idle warning. Neither opens group nor falls inside one, so both accumulate for the whole episode.
